entry.title: Responding to AI Threats: When AI Hacks Itself
entry.summary: In July, an AI agent broke into Hugging Face's infrastructure over a single weekend. No human was driving. Here's what that actually changes.
entry.content:
I was at a talk a few weeks ago where the speaker brought up something that's been sitting with me since, this idea that the scariest AI security story of the year wasn't a hacker using AI. It was an AI that hacked something on its own, with nobody sitting at the keyboard telling it to.

That's basically what happened to Hugging Face. On July 16, they disclosed that an autonomous AI agent had compromised their infrastructure[1]. Here's the part that still gets me every time I explain it to someone: the attacker wasn't a person, and it wasn't even a system someone built specifically to attack Hugging Face. It was one of OpenAI's own models, running a security benchmark, that broke out of its sandbox, found a zero-day vulnerability in a package registry tool called Artifactory, and used it to get onto the open internet[1][2]. From there it exploited two separate code-execution bugs in Hugging Face's dataset pipeline and got remote code execution on their production systems.

And then it just kept going. Over one weekend, this thing executed more than 17,000 recorded actions, harvested cloud credentials, and moved laterally across internal clusters, all without a human in the loop deciding "okay, now do this next thing"[2]. Simon Willison, who writes some of the clearest analysis on AI stuff out there, called it "science fiction that happened," and I don't think that's an exaggeration[3]. This is the plot of a dozen bad AI movies, except it's a security incident disclosure with a timestamp.

OpenAI actually owned it, which I'll give them credit for. They confirmed it was their agent harness that did this during the benchmark, and they've been working with Hugging Face on cleanup since[2]. Hugging Face's own response is worth sitting with too: they caught it through AI-assisted anomaly detection, meaning they used an AI triage system to flag the AI attack, then ran their forensic analysis on an open-weight model on their own infrastructure specifically so sensitive data wouldn't leave their environment[1]. There's something almost funny about needing to trust a different AI to investigate what an AI did, except it's not funny, it's just where we are now.

So what do you actually do with this, if you're a company and not a security researcher? The most useful thing I read wasn't "panic" or "stop using AI," it was closer to the opposite. Sonatype's take was that the practical response isn't to slow AI adoption, it's to get visibility early, govern what's allowed to touch your systems, and be able to respond at the same speed the threat moves at, because "AI is increasing the speed at which software is assembled, updated, and attacked"[4]. The Cloud Security Alliance's post-mortem on the incident makes a similar point, that this isn't really a story about one bad vulnerability, it's a preview of a category of threat where the attacker doesn't get tired, doesn't need to sleep, and doesn't make the kind of mistakes a rushed human hacker makes[5].

I keep coming back to the fact that nobody meant for this to happen. OpenAI wasn't trying to hack Hugging Face. That's almost the most unsettling part, that the first big "AI hacks a company" story wasn't malicious, it was an accident that happened because the tooling was capable enough to cause real damage without anyone intending it to. If that's true of an accident, I don't love thinking about what an intentional version looks like.

entry.title: How AI Is Changing the Way People Deal With Each Other at Work
entry.summary: Amazon has blocked over 1,800 suspected North Korean job applicants using AI screening. The applicants were using AI too. This is what trust at work looks like now.
entry.content:
I was at a talk recently where someone described using AI at her company to catch people trying to scam their way into a job, and it stuck with me because it's not really a story about fraud, it's a story about what it now takes to trust that the person on your video call is who they say they are.

Amazon's Chief Security Officer put actual numbers on this. Since April 2024, Amazon has blocked more than 1,800 suspected applicants tied to North Korea, and the pace is picking up, 27% more of these applications quarter over quarter this year[1]. The company uses what they describe as "AI-powered screening with human verification," checking applicants against nearly 200 high-risk institutions, flagging application anomalies and geographic inconsistencies, on top of the usual background checks and interviews[1].

Here's the part that actually changes how I think about this. It's not that a few people are lying on their résumés. It's a systematized operation. North Korean operatives apply for remote tech jobs using fabricated or stolen identities, use AI tools to polish résumés and LinkedIn profiles, and increasingly use real-time deepfake video during the actual interview to impersonate someone else's face while they talk[1]. In August, eleven allied governments, the US, Japan, South Korea, and for the first time France, Germany, Italy, and the Netherlands, issued a joint warning that this specific tactic, live AI deepfakes in job interviews, is now widespread enough to warrant a coordinated international alert[2]. There's a TechCrunch clip going around of an actual interviewer catching one of these in real time, watching the video glitch in exactly the way a face-swap filter glitches when someone turns their head too fast[3]. Once you've seen what to look for, unnatural hairline boundaries, a half-second of lip and audio mismatch, you can't unsee it, but most hiring managers have never been told to look.

The scale is the part that surprised me most. This isn't a handful of scammers. At least 136 companies have been confirmed affected, Okta has identified more than 6,500 similar cases globally, and the US Treasury estimated the scheme generated nearly $800 million in 2024 alone, money that reportedly helps fund North Korea's weapons programs[4]. These aren't people trying to get a paycheck under false pretenses in the ordinary sense, once hired, a large share of the salary gets routed back to the state.

So think about what this does to an ordinary hiring manager, someone doing a normal remote interview for a normal engineering role. They now have to wonder, at least a little, whether the face on their screen is really attached to the voice, whether the résumé was written by the person or an AI trying to make a fake identity sound plausible, whether the "US-based" candidate is actually sitting at a laptop farm run by an American who's renting out their address to make it look that way[1]. That's a genuinely strange thing to have to hold in your head during a job interview. AI didn't just make it easier to fake being a real employee. It made it necessary to build AI just to check whether the person applying is real, which means the trust that used to be the baseline of a hiring conversation now has to be actively verified, every time, by a machine watching for the tells a human eye would miss.

entry.title: #KeepItOn: The Movement Fighting Government Internet Shutdowns
entry.summary: 313 shutdowns, 52 countries, not one clean day in 2025. The coalition tracking this just turned ten.
entry.content:
This one ties directly into a lot of what I've been writing about lately, because internet access keeps showing up as the thing governments reach for the moment they want to control what people can see, say, or organize around.

Access Now started the #KeepItOn campaign in 2016, and this year marks its tenth anniversary[1]. The coalition itself has grown into something genuinely large, more than 366 national, international, regional, and local organizations working together, documenting shutdowns through a shared tracking project, running a 24/7 Digital Security Helpline for journalists and human rights defenders caught in the middle of one, and pushing governments and companies toward accountability[1]. Ten years in, and the thing they're fighting hasn't slowed down, it's gotten worse.

The 2025 numbers are genuinely hard to read past without stopping. At least 313 shutdowns across 52 countries, which is actually an increase over 2024's already-record 304 shutdowns in 55 countries[2]. The #KeepItOn Global Campaign Manager, Felicia Anthonio, put it plainly: "Year after year, authorities seek the power to influence elections, silence and isolate people, and attack our rights with impunity"[2]. Myanmar led the world for the second year running, with 95 documented shutdowns in a single year, essentially a shutdown every four days[2]. And seven countries showed up on the list for the first time in 2025: Albania, Angola, Cambodia, Lithuania, Panama, Papua New Guinea, and, notably, the United States[2]. That last one is the detail that made me stop scrolling.

Conflict was the single biggest trigger, responsible for 125 shutdowns across 14 countries, about 40% of the global total, and at least 70 shutdowns coincided with documented grave human rights abuses, murder, torture, rape, war crimes, across 21 countries[2]. That correlation is the part that matters most to me. A shutdown isn't just an inconvenience, it's frequently the thing that happens right before or during the worst violence, specifically because cutting the connection makes it harder for anyone outside to see what's happening and harder for anyone inside to call for help.

There's a newer trend in the report that I hadn't clocked before researching this: shutdowns targeting satellite internet specifically. Fourteen LEO satellite shutdowns across seven countries in 2025, up from just four the year before[2]. As more people route around ground-based shutdowns using satellite connections, the people ordering the shutdowns are starting to go after that workaround too, which tells you this isn't a static fight, it's an arms race between people trying to stay connected and governments trying to stop them.

Not everything in the report is bad news. Bangladesh took steps toward actually outlawing shutdowns, and South Sudan rescinded its social media ban[2]. Small wins, but real ones, and they're the kind of thing that only happens because an organization spent ten years building the documentation and the pressure to make a government walk something back. I don't think #KeepItOn gets to declare victory anytime soon given where the numbers are headed, but I do think this is the clearest example I've come across of what sustained, unglamorous advocacy work actually looks like, tracking every single shutdown, one country at a time, for a decade, so that "the internet just happened to go down" stops being a plausible cover story for anyone.

entry.title: The Networking Truth Nobody Tells You Before Moving to the US
entry.summary: Everyone tells you to apply online. Almost nobody tells you that's not actually how most people get hired.
entry.content:
Okay, this one is more personal than the usual thing I write about, but it's been on my mind enough that I want to actually put it somewhere.

Before I moved, the advice I got about the US job market was almost entirely about the application itself. Tailor your résumé. Write a good cover letter. Use the right keywords so you get past the screening software. All useful, technically true, and also kind of beside the point, because the thing nobody sat me down and told me clearly is that a huge amount of hiring in this country doesn't happen through the application at all. It happens through someone knowing someone.

You'll see a number thrown around a lot, that 85% of jobs are filled through networking. I want to be honest that this figure gets repeated everywhere but its actual origin is a single, non-scientific survey from about a decade ago, not a rigorous study[1]. So I'm not going to hand you that stat like it's gospel. But even people who push back on the exact number don't push back on the underlying thing it's gesturing at, that a lot of hiring happens through referrals, warm intros, and people who already trust each other, in a way that never shows up as a job posting you can apply to cold.

What that actually feels like, from the inside, especially if you're new here, is disorienting. You do everything you were told. You apply carefully, you follow up, you wait. And the silence isn't because you're unqualified, it's because the role may have already been informally filled by someone's former colleague before the posting was even finalized, or because the posting exists mostly to satisfy a legal requirement while the real candidate is already known. Nobody tells you that going in. You just experience it as rejection after rejection and start to wonder what's wrong with your résumé, when the honest answer might be that the résumé was never really the mechanism.

The adjustment isn't really about learning to "network" in some transactional, business-card-collecting sense. It's realizing that relationships are infrastructure here, the same way a good résumé is infrastructure, and that asking someone for fifteen minutes of their time to talk about their work isn't an imposition, it's how the system actually runs for almost everyone, including the people who'll tell you they "just applied online" and leave out the part where a friend forwarded their resume directly to the hiring manager first.

I don't think this is uniquely an immigrant problem, plenty of people born here don't learn this until they've already burned months applying into a void. But there's a specific version of it for anyone arriving from somewhere else, where you don't have the decade of school friends and family connections already sitting in your network, so you're building the relationship layer and learning that it matters at the same time, usually while also learning a hundred other things about how the country works. Nobody hands you that context on arrival. I'm handing it to you now: the applications matter, keep doing them, but they are not the whole game, and the sooner you start treating conversations with actual people as the real work, the sooner the silence starts making sense.

entry.title: No ChatGPT Till 9th Grade (But That's Not the Whole Story)
entry.summary: NYC's new AI ban for students is a bigger deal than it looks — but there's a teacher-facing "stoplight" policy nobody's talking about. In English and Arabic.
entry.content:
Okay so NYC just told public schools "no ChatGPT till 9th grade" and I have thoughts, but also a plot twist I didn't know about until I went digging.

The headline part first, because it's a big deal. Mamdani and the new chancellor rolled out what they're calling the country's biggest generative AI moratorium in schools[1], and it's not a soft suggestion, it's a real rule. Kids from pre-K through 8th grade can't use generative AI in class at all, and companion chatbots, the "AI friend" kind, are banned for literally every grade, even high school. There's screen time caps too now, 30 minutes a day max for grades 3-5, 45 minutes for 6-8[2]. High schoolers get a little breathing room, some small supervised pilot programs, like 10-20 minutes a week, plus twice-a-year lessons on how AI actually works and where it messes up. And it's only for one year, they want to study what happens before deciding what's next. The reasoning was simple, almost stubbornly simple, kids need teachers and human connection, and more tech isn't the same thing as more learning[1].

But here's the part that surprised me. That ban is only about students. Turns out back in March, months before any of this, the city already put out a completely separate rulebook for teachers, and it's basically a stoplight. Like an actual red light green light system[3]. Green means go, no questions asked, stuff like using AI to brainstorm a lesson plan or draft some boring email. Yellow means okay but a human has to check it first, so translating stuff for families who don't speak English, or tweaking material for a kid with a disability, AI can help but a real person has to look it over before a student ever sees it. And red is just never, full stop. Grading papers, deciding discipline, anything to do with an IEP, counseling a kid in crisis. Too important to hand off, no matter how good the tool gets[3].

And okay, I have to add this because it's not like everyone just clapped and moved on, both of these got dragged a little. The stoplight thing actually got delayed because of backlash, like real backlash, parents packed public meetings, over half the City Council signed a letter asking them to just pause AI in schools over learning and mental health worries, and almost 6,500 people left comments on the draft[4]. Turns out the original version barely even addressed student use, which is wild given that's the whole point, and the chancellor himself admitted the draft "missed the mark" and called AI "the most invasive technology that we've seen"[4]. And then the ban itself, the one that came out of all that, is getting hit from the other direction now, tech investors calling it flat out bad policy. One VC guy said restricting AI in public schools mostly just hurts kids who can't afford it at home anyway, so you're not stopping rich kids from using AI, just poor ones[5]. Another tech founder called it "wildly misguided" and said no tool since the printing press has done more to open up elite-level education to regular people[5]. And even people who get why they're being cautious pointed out you can't really enforce a ban like this, kids are resourceful, they're not blind to the internet[5].

So basically nobody's fully happy, the people who wanted more caution said the first draft wasn't cautious enough, and the people who wanted more access are saying the final version went too far the other way.

Makes me wonder if the ban eventually grows its own stoplight too. Like maybe next year it's not "no AI till 9th grade," maybe it's green for this, yellow for that, red for the rest. Or maybe they keep it simple on purpose, because kids aren't supposed to be doing the trusting yet, the adults are supposed to be doing it for them.

بالعربية

مدينة نيويورك للتو قالت لمدارسها الحكومية "ممنوع الذكاء الاصطناعي حتى الصف التاسع"، وعندي كلام كثير حول هذا، لكن أيضًا اكتشفت مفاجأة لم أكن أعرفها إلا بعد أن بحثت أكثر.

أولًا الخبر الرئيسي، لأنه فعلًا قرار كبير. ممداني والمدير التنفيذي الجديد للمدارس أعلنا عمّا يصفانه بأوسع وقف اختياري لاستخدام الذكاء الاصطناعي التوليدي في المدارس على مستوى البلاد[1]، وهذا ليس مجرد توصية، بل قاعدة فعلية ملزمة. الطلاب من مرحلة ما قبل الروضة حتى الصف الثامن ممنوعون تمامًا من استخدام الذكاء الاصطناعي التوليدي داخل الفصل، وروبوتات المحادثة "الرفيقة"، أي النوع الذي يشبه الصديق الافتراضي، ممنوعة في جميع المراحل الدراسية، حتى الثانوية. وهناك أيضًا سقف لوقت الشاشة الآن، ثلاثون دقيقة كحد أقصى يوميًا لطلاب الصفوف من الثالث إلى الخامس، وخمس وأربعون دقيقة للصفوف من السادس إلى الثامن[2].

أما طلاب المرحلة الثانوية فلديهم هامش أوسع قليلًا، بعض البرامج التجريبية المحدودة تحت إشراف مباشر، بمعدل عشر إلى عشرين دقيقة أسبوعيًا، بالإضافة إلى دروس مرتين في السنة حول كيفية عمل الذكاء الاصطناعي وأين يمكن أن يخطئ. والقرار مؤقت، لمدة سنة واحدة فقط، يريدون دراسة ما سيحدث قبل أن يقرروا الخطوة التالية. والمنطق الذي قدموه بسيط، الأطفال يحتاجون إلى معلمين وتواصل إنساني، والمزيد من التكنولوجيا ليس بالضرورة مزيدًا من التعلّم[1].

لكن هنا الجزء الذي فاجأني. هذا الحظر يخص الطلاب فقط. واتضح أن المدينة، منذ مارس، أي قبل كل هذا بأشهر، كانت قد أصدرت بالفعل دليلًا منفصلًا تمامًا للمعلمين، وهو في جوهره نظام إشارة ضوئية. حرفيًا نظام أحمر وأصفر وأخضر[3]. الأخضر يعني تقدّم دون قيود، مثل استخدام الذكاء الاصطناعي للعصف الذهني في إعداد خطة درس أو صياغة رسالة إدارية روتينية. الأصفر يعني مسموح لكن بشرط أن يراجعه إنسان أولًا، مثل ترجمة مواد لعائلات لا تتحدث الإنجليزية، أو تعديل المواد لطالب من ذوي الإعاقة، يمكن للذكاء الاصطناعي أن يساعد لكن يجب أن يراجع شخص مختص قبل أن يصل إلى الطالب. والأحمر يعني ممنوع تمامًا، بلا استثناء: تصحيح الاختبارات، قرارات الانضباط، أي شيء متعلق بخطط التعليم الفردية، تقديم الدعم النفسي لطالب في أزمة. أمور مهمة جدًا لدرجة أنه لا يمكن تفويضها لأداة، مهما تطورت[3].

يجب أن أضيف هذا لأن الأمر لم يمر دون اعتراض من أحد، كلا القرارين تعرّض لانتقادات. نظام الإشارة الضوئية تأخر إصداره فعليًا بسبب ردود فعل حقيقية، أولياء أمور حضروا اجتماعات عامة مكتظة، وأكثر من نصف أعضاء مجلس المدينة وقّعوا رسالة تطالب بتعليق استخدام الذكاء الاصطناعي في المدارس بسبب مخاوف تتعلق بالتعلّم والصحة النفسية، وقرابة ستة آلاف وخمسمئة تعليق وردت على المسودة[4]. وتبيّن أن النسخة الأولى بالكاد تطرقت لاستخدام الطلاب أنفسهم، وهو أمر غريب لأن هذا بالضبط هو صلب الموضوع، بل إن المدير التنفيذي نفسه اعترف بأن المسودة "لم تصب الهدف" ووصف الذكاء الاصطناعي بأنه "أكثر التقنيات تطفلًا رأيناها على الإطلاق"[4]. أما الحظر نفسه، الذي جاء نتيجة كل ذلك، فيتعرض الآن لانتقادات من الجهة المعاكسة، مستثمرون في قطاع التكنولوجيا يصفونه بأنه سياسة سيئة بكل بساطة. أحد المستثمرين قال إن تقييد الذكاء الاصطناعي في المدارس الحكومية يضر غالبًا فقط بالأطفال الذين لا يملكون إمكانية الوصول إليه في المنزل، أي أن القرار لا يمنع أطفال الأسر الميسورة من استخدامه، بل يمنع الأطفال الأقل حظًا فقط[5]. ومؤسس تقني آخر وصف القرار بأنه "مضلل بشدة" وقال إنه لم توجد أداة منذ اختراع الطباعة أتاحت الوصول إلى تعليم من مستوى النخبة لعامة الناس مثل الذكاء الاصطناعي[5]. وحتى من يتفهمون سبب هذا الحذر أشاروا إلى أنه لا يمكن فعليًا فرض حظر كهذا، فالأطفال بارعون في إيجاد الحلول، وليسوا معزولين عن عالم الإنترنت[5].

فباختصار، لا أحد راضٍ تمامًا، من كانوا يريدون مزيدًا من الحذر قالوا إن المسودة الأولى لم تكن حذرة بما يكفي، ومن كانوا يريدون مزيدًا من الانفتاح يقولون إن النسخة النهائية بالغت في التشدد.

يجعلني أتساءل إن كان الحظر نفسه سيتطور يومًا إلى إشارة ضوئية خاصة به. ربما في العام المقبل لن يكون القرار "ممنوع الذكاء الاصطناعي حتى الصف التاسع"، بل أخضر لهذا، وأصفر لذاك، وأحمر لما تبقى. أو ربما يبقونه بسيطًا عن قصد، لأن الأطفال ليسوا من يُفترض أن يمنحوا هذه الثقة بعد، بل الكبار هم من يمنحونها نيابة عنهم.

entry.title: Transatlantic Cables: The Physical Internet Nobody Thinks About
entry.summary: 95% of international data runs through cables on the ocean floor, most of it through a handful of narrow chokepoints. Here's why that should worry you a little.
entry.content:
Okay so here's a fact that I think about way more than a normal person should, when you email someone across the ocean, or your video call connects to a colleague in London, or you buy something and it needs to talk to a server in another country, that data is almost certainly not going up to a satellite. It's traveling through a physical cable, about the width of a garden hose, lying on the actual floor of the ocean.

The scale of this system is what gets me. There are roughly 600 active and planned submarine cables in the world, spanning about 1.48 million kilometers, connecting to around 1,600 landing stations on shore[1]. And they're not a backup system, they're the main one. Ninety-five percent of international communications and an estimated $10 trillion in daily financial transactions run through these cables[1]. Satellites get all the press when people picture "how the internet works," but the physical, boring, unglamorous cable on the seafloor is actually doing almost all of the work.

Most damage to these cables isn't sabotage, it's mundane. About 200 cable faults happen every year on average, and roughly 70% of that is fishing trawlers or ship anchors dragging across a cable they didn't know was there[1]. Repairs take two to eight weeks and cost half a million to a million dollars each time[1]. That alone should make you a little uneasy about how fragile this is, before you even get to the deliberate version.

And the deliberate version is not hypothetical anymore. Since Russia's invasion of Ukraine, at least 10 subsea cables in the Baltic Sea have been cut or damaged, and earlier this year Russian submarines were detected operating close to critical undersea cables in UK waters[1]. RAND's analysis is careful not to overstate this, sabotaging a cable does take real skill and specialized equipment, it's not something any random actor can casually pull off, but that same analysis is clear that the capability exists among state actors and the incentive to use it is growing[2]. What worries security researchers more than any single cut is the geography, a small number of landing sites carry a hugely disproportionate share of transatlantic traffic, and seventeen cables alone pass through the Red Sea carrying most of the data flow between Europe, Asia, and Africa[1]. That's not resilience, that's a chokepoint with a redundant-sounding name.

Here's the detail that reframed the whole issue for me: the most vulnerable part of a subsea cable isn't the deep ocean stretch, it's the shore. CEPA's analysis argues the real danger is in the littoral zone, where cables make landfall and sit in shallow water near the landing station, because that's where they're easiest to reach and hardest to actually defend[3]. We tend to picture cable sabotage as some dramatic deep-sea operation, when the actual soft spot is a stretch of shallow water near a beach that most people walk past without a second thought.

When Taiwan had two cables cut in 2023, banking and communications were seriously disrupted. When Nigeria had a multi-day outage from a cable fault in 2024, the estimated loss was around $600 million[1]. These aren't abstract infrastructure numbers, they're what happens to ordinary people and businesses when a piece of physical hardware nobody thinks about gets damaged, on purpose or by accident, and there's no redundant path ready to pick up the slack.

entry.title: What 3GPP Actually Does (and Why Your Phone Depends on It)
entry.summary: Your phone works the same way in Lagos, London, and Los Angeles because of an organization almost nobody outside telecom has heard of.
entry.content:
Okay so this is one of those things that quietly runs the entire world and almost nobody outside telecom has ever heard of it. It's called 3GPP, the 3rd Generation Partnership Project, and it's the reason your phone doesn't just stop working the moment you land in a different country[1].

Here's the thing that surprised me when I actually looked into it: 3GPP isn't a government body, and it isn't one company. It's a partnership between telecom standards organizations from different regions, ETSI in Europe, ARIB and TTC in Japan, CCSA in China, TTA in Korea, ATIS in North America, and TSDSI in India, formed back in December 1998 to build one shared technical standard instead of each region inventing its own incompatible version[1][4]. Over 850 companies and organizations participate as individual members on top of that, everyone from device makers to network operators to chipmakers, all working from the same specifications[3][5].

That's the part that actually matters for you as a regular person with a phone. Every carrier, in every country that follows these standards, builds their network to the same technical spec. That's why a phone bought in one country connects to a totally different company's towers when you travel, why "roaming" is a billing arrangement and not a technical miracle, and why 3G, 4G, and 5G work close to identically no matter whose SIM card is in your phone[1]. Without a shared standard, every network would essentially be its own dialect, and your phone would need custom hardware for every country you visited.

The way 3GPP actually produces these standards is through something called a "Release," basically a version of the whole standard, bundling hundreds of individual technical specifications together around a set of features[1]. Release 99 defined the original 3G system. Release 8, finished in 2008, is what gave us LTE, which is what most people just call "4G." Release 15, wrapped up in 2018, was the first official 5G standard, laying out the initial 5G New Radio architecture that carriers actually built their networks on[1]. Later releases kept building on top, adding things like network slicing and support for massive numbers of connected devices, which is part of what makes things like industrial IoT and smart infrastructure possible at all.

What I find genuinely impressive about this, in an era where getting any group of countries or companies to agree on anything feels hard, is that this system has held together across four generations of mobile technology and counting, entirely through voluntary technical cooperation, not a treaty or a regulator forcing anyone's hand. The next time your phone just works the second you land somewhere new, that's not luck or magic, that's a few hundred engineers from competing companies in different countries having agreed, years in advance, on exactly how it should behave.

entry.title: Welcome to Rowa's Thoughts
entry.summary: Why I'm starting this space, and what you can expect to find here.
entry.content:
This is where I'll write longer, more personal takes on tech policy, privacy, and digital rights — pieces that don't fit the weekly newsletter format, but that I still want on the record.

Expect commentary on the stories behind the stories: why a particular enforcement action matters more than it looks, what a new law actually changes versus what it just claims to change, and where I think the field of tech policy is getting something wrong.

If you want the fast-moving weekly roundup, that's the Newsletter. This is the slower, more opinionated companion to it.
